lokalfinder_grass.//pinHashes: Salted hashes of vendor PINs. NOT readable — this is what stops someone lifting every vendor's credential. Note the app seeds the six DEMO vendors' hashes in index.html itself, so those six are public regardless; rotate them from the admin panel before a real vendor uses one.
lokalfinder_grass.//pinHashes-CONFLICT: DO NOT PUBLISH THIS FILE UNMODIFIED WITHOUT READING THIS. Verified by reading index.html: verifyVendorPin(vid,pin) (~L5853) checks ONLY the in-memory VENDOR_PIN_HASHES object — it never fetches one vendor's hash on demand. VENDOR_PIN_HASHES is populated from two places: the six hardcoded DEMO seeds at boot, and lfFetchScoped() (~L10451), which does a single UNFILTERED fbGet(ROOM_KEY+'/pinHashes') as part of every catalog sync. With .read:false here, that GET returns permission-denied, lfFetchScoped()'s .catch(()=>null) silently swallows it, VENDOR_PIN_HASHES never receives real data, and verifyVendorPin() finds nothing for ANY vendor created after the six demo seeds — every real vendor's PIN is rejected as 'wrong' on any device that has not already cached it (a restored lf-vsess session survives; a fresh login does not). This is a genuine, unresolved conflict between this ruleset and the app's current architecture, not a rules bug — the correct fix is Firebase Auth (a server-verified PIN check, or per-vendor scoped read keyed to a real uid), which is a real architecture change and is intentionally NOT attempted here. Scoping this to a per-vendor exact-key read ($vid.read:true, like orders.$oid) would NOT meaningfully help either: vendor ids are already fully public via the world-readable /vendors node, so per-key access would be trivially equivalent to bulk access for the handful of vendors this app has — the real protection this node provides would be gone either way. Until Firebase Auth exists: publishing this file as-is breaks login for every non-demo vendor on a fresh device. Test in the Rules Playground against a real vendor id created after the six demo seeds before publishing to production.
lokalfinder_grass.//pins: LEGACY plaintext PINs from before v55. Left writable so the app can clear it, but never readable again. Delete this node entirely once every vendor has signed in once and been migrated to pinHashes.
lokalfinder_grass.//adminAuth: Salted hash of the admin password. The in-app admin login reads this to compare, so it must stay readable — meaning the HASH is public. That is survivable because it is salted and you are told to use 8+ characters, but it is a real reason to move admin to Firebase Auth rather than trusting this screen. Verified in index.html (adminCompleteSetup/saveAdminSettings): .write must stay open with no owner check — there is no auth to gate it on, and the app's own 'unclaimed account' bootstrap flow depends on a stranger-writable node to let the founder claim it at all. That means ANYONE can overwrite this record outright (full account takeover, not just an offline hash-crack) until Firebase Auth exists — worse than 'the hash is public' alone. No rules-only fix exists for that; the length caps below only stop a junk/oversized payload, they do not restore ownership.
lokalfinder_grass.//orders: THE IMPORTANT ONE. Without Firebase Auth a rule cannot tell one customer from another, so it cannot say 'read only your own orders'. What it CAN do is refuse an UNFILTERED read: the .read below only passes for a query filtered by vendorId, which is exactly what a signed-in vendor's app sends. A plain GET /orders.json returns permission-denied, so nobody can dump every customer's name, unit and phone in one request. A customer reads their own orders by exact key via the $oid rule. NEXT STEP: switch to Firebase Anonymous Auth and key orders by uid — that is the only way to make this genuinely per-user.

$oid.//lock: genOrderId() (index.html) is a timestamp + small counter + ONE random base36 digit — guessable/brute-forceable, not a real secret — and .write above has no owner check, so anyone who lands on an existing $oid can still write it. Checked every place index.html writes an EXISTING order (updateOrderStatus, adminUpdateStatus, customerCancelOrder): all three only ever change status/updatedAt/acceptedAt/declinedAt/deliveredAt/declinedBy/cancelledByCustomer, and pushOrders() always PUTs the full local object, so every other field is re-sent byte-identical on every legitimate write. So each field below is now locked to its original value once the order exists (data.parent().exists()) — a legitimate write always resends the same value and passes; a guessed/brute-forced id can no longer rewrite someone else's name, phone, unit, building/instructions, total, or which vendor/order the row belongs to. status is deliberately left open post-creation — vendors and admin must be able to change it, and without auth a rule still cannot tell 'the real vendor' from 'anyone holding the id' either way, so this does not close that narrower risk. items/subtotal/method/svcDate/svcTime/kind fall through to $other, unlocked: no write site touches them post-creation either (verified by search), but they were not each individually confirmed field-by-field the way the ones below were, so left as-is rather than guessed at.

lokalfinder_grass.//notifs: Per-recipient node. Not enumerable, so one customer cannot list another's alerts.
lokalfinder_grass.//vendorApplications: v61 self-serve vendor signup. READABLE, and that is a real cost: it holds applicants' names and mobile numbers, so anyone with this URL can read them. It has to be readable because the admin queue must LIST pending applications and there is no auth to scope that read to the admin. Accepted deliberately, and it is one more reason to move to Firebase Auth. Length caps below blunt the obvious spam. WRITE is also open, so a stranger can overwrite or delete SOMEONE ELSE'S pending application — rules cannot stop that without auth to tell one anonymous writer from another. Same class as /vendors and /menu, which are equally open today; the cost here is that a rival could quietly delete a competitor's application. Real fix: Firebase Auth. The PIN is stored as a SALTED HASH the applicant computed on their own device — the plaintext is never transmitted — but a short PIN's hash is brute-forceable from here, which is why the signup form demands 6+ digits where the admin form allows 4.
